newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Aid chiefs to meet in Geneva for Zaire action.
newsitem.headline: Aid chiefs to meet in Geneva for Zaire action.

text.p: Western aid chiefs, donors and relief agencies, debating for weeks what to do with hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees lost in east Zaire, will meet in Geneva on Saturday to coordinate their efforts.

Canadian diplomats said on Wednesday the meeting, chaired by Ottawa's international cooperation minister Don Boudria, would focus on efforts to integrate half a million Hutu refugees who poured back into their tiny Central African homeland.

The Geneva gathering, called as Western countries wavered over plans to deploy a multi-national force in the region, will be the last of three meetings due to be held this week to assess the changing situation in Africa's troubled Great Lakes region.

Another meeting in New York on Wednesday also called by Canada was reviewing plans for a multinational intervention force for Zaire -- despite Washington backing out and many other countries getting cold-feet after many refugees went home.

In Stuttgart, Germany, military officials from 14 nations including France, the United States, Britain and Canada had been due to meet to decide the type of force needed in Zaire. The meeting has now been postponed to Thursday or Friday.

In Geneva, aid officials will try to mobilise donor support for safe and peaceful re-integration of the Hutus, who fled their country in fear of retribution for 1994's Hutu-led genocide of Tutsis, a Canadian official said.

U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) chief Brian Atwood, head of the U.N. refugee agency Sadako Ogata and International Committee of the Red Cross president Cornelio Sommaruga will attend the one-day meeting, he added.
High-level representatives from European donor countries as well as Rwanda's Foreign Minister Anastase Gasana were also expected, he said.
But representatives from the government of Zaire, where aid agencies have yet to have access to another half a million Rwandan Hutu refugees in the east, were not invited to Geneva.
"The purpose of the meeting is to seek agreement on key priorities and coordinate international efforts," the official said. "It will address regional issues but the focus will be on Rwanda."

Rwanda's new Tutsi rulers who took power after the 1994 slaughter face the daunting task of resettling the refugees in Africa's most crowded country where genocide wounds are still fresh and Hutus and Tutsis fear and mistrust each other.

Diplomats fear the mass return will increase ethnic tensions in Rwanda, where 90,000 Hutus are packed into overcrowded jails accused of genocide and a justice system destroyed during the latest Tutsi-Hutu civil war is being built from scratch.
